title: No Verified Record Can Defend Vietnam’s Dog-Meat Supply Chain
excerpt: A stolen companion, poisoned bait, or infected shipment demands proof—not slogans. Without inspection and traceability, public safety cannot rest on trade assurances.
body_html:
A family dog stolen from its home, a poisoned bait left where residents walk, or an uninspected shipment can turn private grief into a public-safety threat. Yet no police record, court judgment, seizure report, or named inspection finding accompanies the trade defenses presented here. That gap matters. Claims about “tradition” or “farm-raised dogs” cannot replace traceability.

Myth needs records

“Farm-raised” is not proof of lawful origin. A credible claim needs breeder records, animal identification, transport documents, quarantine compliance, veterinary inspection, and a chain of custody from birth to slaughter. Without those records, no reader can distinguish lawful production from stolen companions or animals moved outside health controls. Do not turn an unsupported defense into a fact.

Biosecurity cannot run on promises

Household rabies exposure and commercial supply-chain failures are separate risks. They share one preventable weakness: poor control of animal movement and delayed reporting. Rabies spreads when infected saliva enters bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. After possible exposure, wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. WHO guidance supports immediate care before symptoms develop.

Vietnamese communities can demand proof

Families deserve protection from theft, unsafe transport, illegal slaughter, and disease risk. That means public records, enforceable quarantine, transparent inspections, and accountability for illicit operators. Public-health targets set by government bodies are not the same as SDE’s campaign demand for complete abolition by 2030. Add your name to that demand: sign the national petition and follow campaign updates reaching decision-makers.
